ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-08-04 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A credential-stealing worm hidden in more than 400 compromised npm packages automatically spread across software ecosystems by republishing malicious updates. This analysis details the attack chain, affected environments, and practical guidance for detection, hunting, and remediation. The post ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Shai-Hulud npm worm: 'node setup.mjs' spawns obfuscated Bun bundle from node_modules/bun-dl- AIInstallation High
Hunts the ChainDrop/Mini Shai-Hulud execution chain where an npm preinstall hook runs setup.mjs (via node) which in turn launches the large obfuscated Bun runtime bundle from a bun-dl- staging folder or inside node_modules. This parent(node,setup.mjs)->child(bun) tree is the article's exact execution fingerprint and is virtually never benign. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim hunting query (code Block 2): InitiatingProcess node + 'setup.mjs' command line spawning a 'bun' child from bun-dl-/node_modules. This exact parent->child tree is the worm's defining execution behaviour and does not occur in normal Node development. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately vendoring the Bun runtime inside a project's node_modules and invoking it from a build script named setup.mjs (rare)
  • Internal tooling that ships a bun-dl- style downloader for CI reproducibility
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox (expected, whitelist the analysis host)
  • Monorepo build orchestrators that shell out from node to bun across workspace packages
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full process tree on the host - confirm the grandparent is npm/npx install and capture the offending package name/version from InitiatingProcessCommandLine and FolderPath; hash the setup.mjs and bun bundle. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the workstation/build runner, kill the detached node/bun processes, and treat every credential reachable from that identity (npm, GitHub, AWS, Kubernetes, Vault) as compromised - begin rotation from a known-clean host. 3) HUNT: Sweep for the IOC hashes (UC2), C2 domains (UC3), editor-config persistence (UC4) and any results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json staging artifacts (UC5) org-wide; enumerate npm packages published by the affected maintainer identity for unauthorized patch releases.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where FolderPath has "bun-dl-" or ProcessCommandLine has "node_modules"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "node_modules" or ActingProcessName has "bun-dl-"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud loader/payload known-bad SHA256 written to disk (setup.mjs, Math_*.js) AIInstallation Medium
Fires when any of the three Microsoft-published ChainDrop hashes are written to disk: the npm tarball preinstall loader setup.mjs (54dc7ea5...), the .claude/.vscode repository loader setup.mjs (fd3ca400...), and the Math_*.js obfuscated component (9fc2570b...). Hash-exact, so it is the highest-fidelity trip-wire for the campaign. Rationale: Uses the three exact SHA256 indicators from the article's IOC table and code Block 3. Hash-exact matches have effectively zero false positives and cover both the npm-tarball loader and the editor-config persistence loader. Falcon left blank: FDR FileWritten does not carry a file-content hash field, so a hash pivot is not expressible there (use UC1/UC6 filename+path pivots on Falcon instead). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/

Shai-Hulud C2 beacon to npm-cache[.]com / pypi-get[.]com / js-mirror[.]com from node/bun AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or outbound connections to the three attacker HTTPS C2 domains used for AES+RSA-encrypted exfiltration, scoped to node/bun initiating processes on developer/build hosts. These typosquat-registry domains are the campaign's primary exfil channel before the GitHub-repo fallback. Rationale: Domains npm-cache[.]com, pypi-get[.]com and js-mirror[.]com are named directly in the article body and IOC table as C2/exfil endpoints. Registry-typosquat domains contacted by node/bun on a dev host are extremely high-fidelity. Sentinel query intentionally omits the process filter because ImDnsActivity has no process context - the domain match alone is sufficient signal. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/a-new-infostealer-worm-hits-npm-affecting-keyv-and-cacheable/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal proxy or DNS sinkhole resolving the domains for blocklisting/telemetry (validate the SrcIp is a security appliance)
  • Threat-intel scanners or URL detonation sandboxes probing the IOCs
  • A developer manually curling the domain to confirm it is malicious during IR
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !has_any ("dns-sinkhole","proxy","ti-scanner")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the host and the initiating node/bun process; confirm whether an encrypted results-*.json was staged and whether the connection succeeded (bytes sent). 2) CONTAIN: Sinkhole/block the three domains at the proxy and firewall, isolate the host, and immediately rotate every credential the identity could reach - assume exfil succeeded. 3) HUNT: Search org-wide DNS for the same domains and for outbound calls to blockchain RPC endpoints that precede the beacon; look for a public GitHub repo created under the identity with description 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'.

  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
   | where RemoteUrl has_any (c2)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="DNS", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP="", RemotePort=int(null), InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("npm-cache.com","pypi-get.com","js-mirror.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud editor-config persistence: setup.mjs written under .claude/ or .vscode/ AIInstallation Medium
Detects the worm's developer-to-developer persistence: injection of loader files into .claude/settings.json, .claude/setup.mjs, .vscode/tasks.json and .vscode/setup.mjs so future editor activity relaunches the payload. A setup.mjs living under an editor-config directory is never legitimate; also matches the fd3ca400 loader hash. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit persistence paths (.claude/settings.json, .claude/setup.mjs, .vscode/tasks.json, .vscode/setup.mjs) plus the fd3ca400 repository-loader hash. Constraining to setup.mjs under editor-config dirs avoids FPs from legitimate settings.json/tasks.json edits while keeping the worm's unique artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/
ATT&CKT1554 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team standardizing on a project bootstrap named setup.mjs and accidentally committing it under .vscode (verify contents are not obfuscated Bun)
  • IR responders restoring a golden .vscode profile that already contains the malicious file
  • Backup/sync tools re-materializing the file during recovery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","code") or SHA256 =~ "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the flagged setup.mjs / settings.json - confirm obfuscated Bun loader content and check git blame/commit author to see if it arrived with no matching PR. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the injected files from all branches, revoke the GitHub token that pushed them, and isolate any host that already opened the poisoned workspace. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every repo the compromised GitHub identity can write to for the same .claude/.vscode injections; correlate with commits lacking an authoring PR.

Shai-Hulud exfil staging: results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json written by node/bun AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the encrypted-exfil staging artifact the worm serializes before shipping over HTTPS or committing to a fallback GitHub repo. Files named results-<digits>-<digits>.json created by a node or bun process are the campaign's collection fingerprint and pair tightly with the C2 signal (UC3). Rationale: The article names the exact staging filename pattern results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json produced during JSON->gzip->AES-256-GCM packaging. Constraining the writer to node/bun keeps it worm-specific and separates it from generic app output. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1567.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A test runner or benchmarking tool that emits timestamped results-<epoch>-<n>.json files from a node process (inspect contents - should be plaintext, not AES blobs)
  • CI pipelines writing node-based coverage/report artifacts with a similar name
  • A data-processing job under Bun that batches output files by counter
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\coverage\\","\\test-results\\","/coverage/","/test-results/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the flagged file - confirm it is an opaque encrypted blob (RSA-wrapped AES) rather than readable JSON, and identify the writing node/bun process. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host before egress completes, rotate all reachable credentials, and block the C2 domains from UC3. 3) HUNT: Correlate the file-create time with outbound connections to npm-cache/pypi-get/js-mirror and with any new public GitHub repo (description 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again') holding results-*.json commits.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^results-\d+-\d+\.json$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^results-\d+-\d+\.json$"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud self-propagation: node/bun injecting setup.mjs / Math_*.js into node_modules packages AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the worm's horizontal spread - a node/bun process writing the loader (setup.mjs) or the Math_Symbol.js / Math_init.js / math_<guid>.js payload component into other packages under node_modules or a bun-dl- staging folder before republishing. Filename+path+writer pivot survives hash rotation, complementing the hash rule (UC2). Rationale: Targets the article's propagation routine (copy malware bundle + loader into each package's node_modules) using the named artifact filenames setup.mjs and Math_Symbol.js/Math_init.js/math_<guid>.js from the detection hints. A node/bun process writing these into node_modules is the worm mutating other packages, not a normal install. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1080
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build/bundler step that legitimately writes a file named setup.mjs into a workspace package during a monorepo publish
  • Postinstall scripts of a trusted package that generate helper .js files inside their own node_modules folder
  • npm pack/publish tooling under Bun re-staging package contents
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","ci","publish","pack") == false
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the target package(s) receiving the write and whether the writing identity holds an npm publish token; hash the written setup.mjs against the UC2 IOCs. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the npm publishing token immediately, isolate the host, and quarantine any packages republished from that identity in the last 30 days. 3) HUNT: Query the npm registry for patch-bumped releases by the maintainer with no matching git commit/PR/tag and pull those tarballs to confirm an added preinstall hook + setup.mjs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "setup.mjs" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^math_(symbol|init)\.js$" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^math_[0-9a-f\-]{8,}\.js$")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" or FolderPath has "bun-dl-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "setup.mjs" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^math_(symbol|init)\.js$" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^math_[0-9a-f\-]{8,}\.js$")
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" or TargetFilePath has "bun-dl-"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud credential harvesting: node/bun reading SSH keys, cloud creds and npm/GitHub tokens AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the worm's local credential collector accessing ~/.ssh keys, cloud config (.aws/credentials, .kube/config, Vault), .npmrc, GitHub CLI hosts.yml and shell histories from a node/bun runtime. Primary telemetry is CrowdStrike FileOpenInfo (file reads); Defender/Sentinel capture the modification/copy variants since XDR does not emit pure-read events. Rationale: Grounded in the article's credential-discovery step: the filesystem collector searches SSH keys, cloud config, shell histories and CLI tokens, and the shell collector grabs the GitHub CLI token. Scoping the reader to node/bun makes it worm-specific. Falcon FileOpenInfo is the authoritative source because Defender/Sentinel XDR do not emit pure file-read events - their queries here catch the modify/copy/exfil-staging variants only (noted for the analyst). Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Node CLI (e.g. an AWS SDK tool, a git helper, or an npm auth flow) reading .aws/credentials or .npmrc during normal use
  • IaC or deployment scripts under Node/Bun reading .kube/config to talk to a cluster
  • Dotfile-management tooling backing up .ssh or shell history
  • Developer setup scripts sourcing shell history
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-sdk","@aws","kubectl","npm login","npm whoami") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/npx install (grandparent) versus an interactive developer tool - install-context reads of .ssh + .aws + .npmrc in one burst is the worm. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host and rotate every credential the identity could reach (SSH keys, AWS, npm, GitHub, Kubernetes, Vault) from a clean environment. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC3/UC5 on the same host for C2 egress and results-*.json staging, and check the AWS/GitHub sides for API enumeration bursts from the harvested identities.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\.ssh\" or FolderPath has "/.ssh/"
      or FolderPath has @"\.aws\" or FolderPath has "/.aws/"
      or FolderPath has @"\.kube\" or FolderPath has "/.kube/"
      or FileName in~ (".npmrc",".git-credentials",".bash_history",".zsh_history")
      or (FolderPath has "gh" and FileName =~ "hosts.yml")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.ssh\" or TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/"
      or TargetFilePath has @"\.aws\" or TargetFilePath has "/.aws/"
      or TargetFilePath has @"\.kube\" or TargetFilePath has "/.kube/"
      or TargetFileName in~ (".npmrc",".git-credentials",".bash_history",".zsh_history")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-sourced enumeration of TP-Link Omada device-adoption ports (29810-29816) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts external hosts probing an internet-exposed Omada controller's zero-touch-provisioning port range (29810 discovery through 29816 rtty). Forescout found 1,800+ controllers reachable this way; these ports are intended for on-LAN device adoption only, so public-internet volume against them is the serial-number/MAC enumeration step of the ZTP attack chain. Rationale: Pivots on the exact Omada ZTP port range (29810 discovery, 29811 manager.v1, 29812 adopt.v1, 29813 upgrade.v1, 29814 manager.v2, 29815 transfer.v2, 29816 rtty) confirmed against TP-Link's own port FAQ, combined with an external-source predicate — this is the concrete shape of the serial/MAC enumeration Forescout described. Cross-checked TP-Link/Omada advisory and port documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/ • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/document/13087/ • https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3281/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/tp-link-patches-four-omada-gateway.html
ATT&CKT1595.001 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide background scanners (Shodan, Censys, GreyNoise) sweeping the 29810-29816 range against an accidentally-exposed controller
  • A legitimate remote MSP performing bulk device adoption over a site-to-site VPN whose egress IP is not in the RFC1918 exclusion list
  • NAT/CGNAT collapsing many internal adoption sessions behind one public IP, inflating the per-source count
  • Security team's own external vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Nessus/Forescout) profiling the controller
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health checks hitting the management ports
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known_scanner_ips_ref_table>"]))     // replace with a watchlist(); optional GreyNoise/known-scanner suppression
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is an Omada controller and whether it is intentionally internet-exposed; check whether the SourceIP is a known scanner (GreyNoise) or a single actor touching multiple adoption ports. 2) Contain: if the controller should not be internet-facing, firewall-block inbound WAN to 29810-29816 (and 8043/8088/8843) immediately and restrict adoption to the management VLAN. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SourceIP for follow-on allowed connections to the adoption port (see the initial-access UC), and review the controller for any device adopted from an external address or duplicate serial/MAC.

| where Conns > 20     // 20 = enumeration threshold; a legit host adopts a device with a handful of packets, not a sweep
| order by Conns desc

| summarize Conns=count(), DistinctPorts=dcount(DestinationPort), DestPorts=make_set(DestinationPort), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP
| where Conns > 20     // 20 = enumeration threshold vs. background single-packet internet scans

Rogue device adoption from the public internet to Omada controller (default-cred/race exploit) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a successful/allowed inbound connection from a non-RFC1918 source to the Omada adoption ports (29812 adopt.v1 / 29814 manager.v2). Legitimate zero-touch adoption always originates from a managed device on the LAN — an allowed adoption handshake sourced from the internet is the device-spoofing + cloud-adoption race condition that lets an attacker authenticate with default credentials (CVE-2025-9290 / CVE-2025-15544 / CVE-2025-15627). Rationale: Anchors on port 29812 (port.adopt.v1) and 29814 (port.manager.v2) with an allowed action from a public source — the exact network signature of Forescout's spoof-a-pending-device + win-the-adoption-race scenario, which is impossible for a legitimately on-LAN device. Ports verified against TP-Link's Omada SDN port FAQ. Defender/Falcon left empty: the controller is a network appliance, not an EDR-onboarded endpoint, so this inbound-to-appliance flow is only visible to the perimeter firewall. Cross-checked against: • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/ • https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3281/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-9289/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-based/off-site Omada controller legitimately adopting remote devices over WAN where those devices' public IPs are expected
  • Remote branch device adopting through a controller whose firewall NATs the branch to a public IP not in the RFC1918 list
  • A misconfigured firewall rule that legitimately forwards WAN traffic to adoption ports for a supported remote-adoption deployment
  • Penetration test or Forescout/BAS tooling replaying the adoption exploit against the controller
Suppression filter
| where DestinationIP !in (dynamic(["<sanctioned_wan_adoption_controller_ips>"]))     // optional: exclude controllers with an approved remote-adoption deployment (watchlist)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP geolocation/ASN and whether any remote-adoption deployment is sanctioned; on the controller, list devices adopted in the alert window and look for a device whose serial/MAC was already present (duplicate/spoof) or that used default credentials. 2) Contain: block inbound WAN to 29812/29814 at the firewall, force-remove the rogue device, and rotate the controller admin password plus any exposed device secrets (cleartext username, MD5 hash, VPN keys). 3) Hunt: from the same SourceIP look for a preceding enumeration burst and subsequent XSS payloads to the admin ports (8043/8088/8843), and audit for newly created VPN tunnels or config pushes.

| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","allowed","permit","accept","Permit")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stored XSS / JavaScript injection into Omada controller admin UI (CVE-2025-9289) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the Omada controller web-admin ports (8043/8088/8843) carrying JavaScript/HTML injection markers. Maps CVE-2025-9289 and CVE-2025-15628 — the attacker persists script in an admin field so an authenticated administrator's browser executes it and phishes their cloud-controller credentials. Rationale: Combines the Omada web-admin ports (8043/8088/8843, per TP-Link's port FAQ) with common XSS injection tokens to catch the CVE-2025-9289/CVE-2025-15628 admin-UI JavaScript injection Forescout used to phish admin credentials. URL/query-based payloads are captured; note stored-XSS via POST body may be missed if the proxy does not log bodies — pair with the ImWebSession table where request bodies are available. Defender/Falcon empty: web request targets the appliance, not an EDR host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-9289/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9289 • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security scanner (Burp/ZAP/Qualys) actively testing the controller for XSS with the same payload tokens
  • A legitimate admin pasting configuration text that happens to contain 'onload=' or 'javascript:' into a controller field
  • URL-encoded query strings in normal portal-authentication flows that coincidentally contain matched substrings
  • WAF logging both the request and its own sanitized copy, double-counting the event
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp", "Nessus", "Qualys", "OWASP ZAP", "nuclei")     // suppress known security-scanner user-agents
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RequestMethod/RequestURL contains an actual injection (decode %3Cscript) versus a scanner probe, and identify whether the SourceIP is internal (admin browser) or external; capture the DestinationIP controller. 2) Contain: if a persisted payload is confirmed, restrict admin-UI access to a management VLAN, patch to the fixed Omada firmware, and invalidate admin sessions plus rotate cloud-controller credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP with prior adoption-port activity, and review controller admin fields/objects for stored script and any anomalous outbound POST of admin credentials to attacker infrastructure.

| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Spoofed RingCentral email delivered to inbox despite SPF/DMARC failure (safe-sender whitelist abuse) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Microsoft 365 device-code authentication flow redeemed (Greatness device-code phishing) · [LLM] RingCentral-phish click followed by MFA-approved M365 sign-in from a new IP (AiTM correlation) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MFA-satisfied M365 token replay from VPS/VPN hosting ASN (Greatness AiTM post-compromise) · [LLM] Connection or sign-in to known Greatness / RingCentral-phish infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk Microsoft Graph resource enumeration from a single hosted session (post-token-replay discovery) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Spoofed RingCentral email delivered to inbox despite SPF/DMARC failure (safe-sender whitelist abuse) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail claiming to be from ringcentral.com (notably service@ringcentral.com) that fails SPF and DMARC and carries no DKIM signature yet still lands in the inbox because RingCentral is on a safe-sender/allow list. This is the exact Greatness delivery vector: whitelist abuse achieving SCL -1 on Exchange. Rationale: Uses the article's precise facts: sender ringcentral.com / service@ringcentral.com, SPF+DMARC fail, no DKIM, delivered to inbox via whitelist. The envelope-domain mismatch is the high-fidelity discriminator between the spoof and genuine RingCentral notifications. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine RingCentral notification emails where an outbound connector/forwarding breaks SPF/DKIM alignment
  • Legitimate RingCentral mail relayed through a third-party marketing platform failing alignment
  • Internal phishing-simulation traffic spoofing RingCentral
  • Mailbox rules auto-forwarding RingCentral notifications and stripping DKIM
Suppression filter
| where SenderIPv4 !in ("104.245.56.0")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SenderMailFromDomain/SenderIPv4 is NOT genuine RingCentral (real notifications use RingCentral SPF ranges, not an IONOS relay); inspect the embedded URL for M365-login lookalikes. 2) Contain: ZAP the message across all recipients, block the sender IP/URL, and pull RingCentral from blanket safe-sender lists - replace with an authenticated-sender rule. 3) Hunt: pivot on NetworkMessageId to UrlClickEvents for any clicker, then check sign-ins for a subsequent MFA-approved logon from hosting/VPN IPs.
let RingCentralClaim = dynamic(["ringcentral.com","service@ringcentral.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ringcentral.com" or SenderFromAddress has "ringcentral"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","Inbox/Folder")
| extend Auth = tolower(tostring(AuthenticationDetails))
| where Auth has "spf=fail" or Auth has "spf=softfail" or Auth has "dmarc=fail" or Auth has "dkim=none" or Auth has "compauth=fail"
| where SenderMailFromDomain !~ "ringcentral.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderIPv4, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, Url, UrlDomain, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let RingCentralClaim = dynamic(["ringcentral.com","service@ringcentral.com"]);
EmailEvents

| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderIPv4, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, Url, UrlDomain, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Microsoft 365 device-code authentication flow redeemed (Greatness device-code phishing) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth 2.0 device-code grant, the second Greatness attack path alongside AiTM. Device-code phishing harvests tokens without the victim entering credentials on the phishing domain, so a first-time device-code redemption on a user is high-signal. Rationale: Article explicitly names a 'device-code phishing flow' as an alternate Greatness path; AuthenticationProcessingDetails carries the grant marker. Aggregating by user surfaces first-time/anomalous device-code redemption, rare in most orgs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://medium.com/@anyrun/greatness-phaas-overview-60776ac601b7
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code login for smart TVs / Teams Rooms / conference devices
  • Developers running 'az login --use-device-code' or Connect-MgGraph device flow
  • IoT / kiosk provisioning using device code
  • CLI tooling on headless servers authenticating via device code
Suppression filter
| where Apps !has "Microsoft Azure CLI" and Apps !has "Microsoft Azure PowerShell"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user's role/device plausibly uses device-code auth; check IPs/ASNs vs known locations and whether a second IP redeemed the token. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), require re-auth, and disable device-code flow for that population via Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: look for immediate post-redemption Graph enumeration from a hosting IP and new OAuth consent grants in the same session.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| extend Proc = tolower(tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails))
| where Proc has "device code" or Proc has "devicecode"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), Apps=make_set(Application,20), Countries=make_set(Country,10) by AccountUpn
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend Proc = tolower(tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails))
| where Proc has "device code" or Proc has "devicecode"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,20), ASNs=make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber,20) by UserPrincipalName
| order by FirstSeen desc
MFA-satisfied M365 token replay from VPS/VPN hosting ASN (Greatness AiTM post-compromise) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts successful, MFA-satisfied but non-interactive Entra sign-ins from commercial VPS/VPN autonomous systems - the signature of Greatness operators replaying an AiTM-captured, MFA-approved token from proxy infrastructure. Access persisted 2+ weeks in observed cases. Rationale: Article: operators 'replayed Microsoft 365 authentication tokens from VPS and commercial VPN infrastructure' with access persisting >2 weeks. Non-interactive + MFA-already-satisfied + hosting ASN is the replay fingerprint; the ASN list and pipeline-extracted IP 38.248.95.214 anchor it. IP not independently second-sourced, hence Medium. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User on a commercial VPN (NordVPN/Mullvad ride M247) accessing M365
  • Corporate SASE/egress through a cloud-hosted proxy sharing a hosting ASN
  • Service accounts running in AWS/Azure/GCP hitting Graph non-interactively
  • Mobile carrier peering via a listed transit ASN
  • Red-team infrastructure in a VPS
Suppression filter
| where Apps !has "Microsoft Azure PowerShell" and UserPrincipalName !startswith "svc-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the hosting-ASN sign-in against the user's baseline; confirm the token was first minted interactively elsewhere (AiTM) and check for concurrent legit sessions. 2) Contain: revoke all tokens, reset password, re-register MFA, add a CA block for the ASN/IP. 3) Hunt: enumerate what the session touched - Graph calls, inbox rules, OAuth consents, file downloads - and sweep other users for the same IP/ASN.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where IsInteractive == false
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high","medium") or IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sessions=count(), Resources=make_set(ResourceDisplayName,20), Apps=make_set(Application,20) by AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country
| where LastSeen - FirstSeen > 1h
| order by FirstSeen desc
let HostingASNs = dynamic([14061,63949,16276,24940,51167,20473,9009,396982,16509,14618,3223,201814]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where IsInteractive == false
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (HostingASNs) or IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Sessions=count(), Resources=make_set(ResourceDisplayName,20), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,20) by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, tostring(LocationDetails)
| order by FirstSeen desc

Bulk Microsoft Graph resource enumeration from a single hosted session (post-token-replay discovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single account/session sweeping across many M365 resource types via Microsoft Graph - mail, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, contacts, calendars, registered apps - in a short window from a hosting/VPN IP. The Greatness post-compromise discovery phase after token replay. Rationale: Article lists the exact Graph-enumerated resources (Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, contacts, calendars, registered apps). Fan-out across >=4 ObjectTypes from a hosting ISP in 1h captures the discovery burst, not normal single-app usage. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas
ATT&CKT1526 T1213 T1087.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned SaaS backup/eDiscovery/DLP tools (Veeam M365, AvePoint) enumerating Graph from cloud infra
  • CASB posture scanners hitting many resource types
  • Migration tooling reading mailboxes/SharePoint during a tenant move
  • Power Automate / Logic Apps flows fanning across resources
  • Admin running Graph PowerShell inventory from an Azure jump box
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has "eDiscovery" and AccountDisplayName !has "Backup" and AccountDisplayName !has "CASB"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the session and whether the IP/ISP is sanctioned automation; correlate to the token-replay UC for the same user. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, block the IP/ASN, and if a rogue OAuth app is the principal, disable and remove its consent. 3) Hunt: review inbox-rule creation, mass OneDrive/SharePoint access, and Teams reads for exfil; check whether other users were enumerated from the same source.
let HostingISP = dynamic(["digitalocean","linode","ovh","hetzner","contabo","vultr","choopa","m247","amazon","microsoft","google","voxility","leaseweb"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Application in~ ("Microsoft Graph","Office 365","Microsoft 365")
| extend ISPl = tolower(tostring(ISP))
| where isnotempty(ISPl) and ISPl has_any (HostingISP)

| where DistinctObjectTypes >= 4 and Ops >= 20
| order by Ops desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where ResourceDisplayName in~ ("Microsoft Graph","Windows Azure Active Directory","Microsoft Graph PowerShell")
| where IsInteractive == false
| summarize GraphSignIns=count(), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,20), ASNs=make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber,10) by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where GraphSignIns >= 15

source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 @properties.resourceDisplayName:("Microsoft Graph" OR "Microsoft Graph PowerShell")
Connection or sign-in to known Greatness / RingCentral-phish infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Direct IOC pivot on the Greatness infrastructure for this campaign: sign-ins from IP 38.248.95.214 and endpoint DNS/network resolution of panel.securehubcloud.com and aitomayu.com. Low-volume, high-specificity confirmation a host or account touched operator infrastructure. Rationale: Pipeline-extracted IOCs for this campaign (IP 38.248.95.214; domains panel.securehubcloud.com, aitomayu.com). Individual indicators not independently second-sourced beyond the campaign, so Medium - treat as a pivot/confirmation, but specificity keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1071.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher/SOC analyst sandboxing the domains from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel platform auto-resolving IOCs for enrichment
  • Shared-hosting IP reassigned to a benign tenant after the campaign
  • Proxy prefetch/URL-preview service resolving the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the querying host/account and whether the touch was human browsing (post click) vs automated enrichment. 2) Contain: block the IP and domains at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the endpoint if a user browsed there, force token revocation for any account signing in from 38.248.95.214. 3) Hunt: back-trace to the delivering RingCentral-spoof email and forward to any MFA-approved sign-in or Graph enumeration tied to the same user.
let IOCIPs = dynamic(["38.248.95.214"]);
let IOCDomains = dynamic(["panel.securehubcloud.com","aitomayu.com"]);
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteIP in (IOCIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (IOCDomains)
 | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceNetwork", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort),
(AADSignInEventsBeta
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where IPAddress in (IOCIPs)
 | project Timestamp, Source="AADSignIn", DeviceName, AccountName=AccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName="", RemoteIP=IPAddress, RemoteUrl=Application, RemotePort=int(null))
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOCIPs = dynamic(["38.248.95.214"]);
let IOCDomains = dynamic(["panel.securehubcloud.com","aitomayu.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress in (IOCIPs) | project TimeGenerated, Source="SigninLogs", Account=UserPrincipalName, Indicator=IPAddress, AppDisplayName),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (IOCDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Account=SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery, AppDisplayName=""),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (IOCIPs) or RequestURL has_any (IOCDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Account=SourceUserName, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationIP), AppDisplayName="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:

level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*securehubcloud.com* OR *aitomayu.com*)) OR (source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" CIDR(@network.client.ip, 38.248.95.214/32))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(securehubcloud\.com|aitomayu\.com)$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
RingCentral-phish click followed by MFA-approved M365 sign-in from a new IP (AiTM correlation) AIExploitation High
Correlates a user clicking the URL inside the spoofed RingCentral email with a successful, MFA-satisfied Entra sign-in shortly after from an unfamiliar IP - the AiTM session-theft outcome. Pairs delivery telemetry with identity telemetry to catch the moment the stolen token is first used. Rationale: Ties the delivery vector (RingCentral-spoof email + click) to its credential-access outcome (AiTM-captured MFA-approved token used to sign in). The 30-minute click-to-sign-in window plus MFA-satisfied success is the AiTM signature and eliminates benign clicks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User clicks a genuine RingCentral link then legitimately signs into M365 from a new but benign location
  • Traveling user clicking then authenticating via corporate VPN egress
  • Safe Links detonation click recorded while a normal sign-in coincidentally occurs
  • Shared workstation where click and sign-in are different people on the same UPN
Suppression filter
| where SignInIP != "" and Country !in ("US","CA","GB","AU","ZA") or DelayMin <= 5
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine SignInIP/Country vs baseline and whether the device is registered/compliant; short DelayMin (<5m) from a new IP is strongest. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, reset password + MFA, block the sign-in IP; ZAP the originating RingCentral-spoof email tenant-wide. 3) Hunt: from the confirmed session pull Graph enumeration, inbox rules, OAuth consents, and repeat sign-ins from the same IP/ASN; sweep other recipients of the same message cluster.
let Lookback = 14d;
let WindowMin = 30m;
let Clicks =
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and (SenderFromDomain =~ "ringcentral.com" or SenderFromAddress has "ringcentral")
    | join kind=inner (UrlClickEvents | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback) | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")) on NetworkMessageId
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp1, AccountUpn, ClickUrl = Url, Subject, SenderFromAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ErrorCode == 0 and AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| join kind=inner Clicks on $left.AccountUpn == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + WindowMin)
| project ClickTime, SignInTime = Timestamp, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ClickTime), AccountUpn, SignInIP = IPAddress, Country, Application, ClickUrl, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by ClickTime desc
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
