Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

    selection_parent_vendor:

Flowise unauthenticated OAuth2 token-refresh endpoint hit (CVE-2026-70478) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces HTTP requests to Flowise's whitelisted, no-auth endpoint POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId. Any such request from a non-internal source (or returning HTTP 200 with a token body) indicates an attacker abusing the WHITELIST_URLS gap to steal OAuth access tokens for a connected Google/Microsoft/GitHub account. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route from the advisory root-cause (packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts) and constants.ts WHITELIST_URLS entry: POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId. Path is Flowise-specific so FP risk is near-zero; external-source filter removes legitimate server-internal refresh traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-70478 • https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/52557
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise UI-driven manual credential refresh performed by an authenticated admin from the corporate network (internal IP — excluded by the private-IP filter)
  • External uptime/synthetic monitors probing the API surface (would 404/400 on fake credential IDs, not 200)
  • Security scanners / authorized pentest traffic hitting the endpoint during an assessment window
  • Reverse proxy or load-balancer health checks that follow a redirect onto the API path
  • CI/CD integration test suites for a self-hosted Flowise instance calling the refresh route
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and csUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and csUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request/response for the matching cIP+csUriStem; confirm HTTP 200 and extract the credentialId from the path. Identify which stored OAuth credential (Google/Microsoft/GitHub) it maps to in Flowise. 2) Contain: upgrade Flowise to 3.1.3 immediately (removes the endpoint from WHITELIST_URLS); revoke and re-issue the affected connected-service OAuth credential (rotate client_secret + refresh_token); block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: search the connected service's own audit logs (AAD SigninLogs / Google Workspace / GitHub audit) for use of the leaked access token from the attacker IP, and review W3CIISLog for the sibling advisories CVE-2026-69250 (SSRF) and CVE-2026-70474 (cross-workspace metadata leak) against the same host.
// Flowise CVE-2026-70478 — external hit on the no-auth OAuth2 refresh endpoint
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))            // external caller = never legitimate for a server-side refresh flow
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent, csReferer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise OAuth2 credentialId enumeration (brute-force of refresh route) AIReconnaissance High
Detects a single source issuing many requests to /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId with distinct credentialId path segments in a short window — the discovery step where an attacker brute-forces valid credential IDs (mix of 200 for valid, 404 'Credential not found' for invalid) before harvesting tokens. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's Docker Validation note (fake-uuid returns 'Credential not found' / 404 rather than 401) and the :credentialId parameter with no described validation — the mix of 200/404 across many distinct path values from one source is the enumeration fingerprint. Threshold of 5 distinct IDs/2min separates it from a legitimate single-credential UI refresh. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-70478
ATT&CKT1190 T1110
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Flowise admin bulk-refreshing many stored credentials from the UI in one sitting (rare; usually authenticated + internal IP)
  • An automated job/cron in the org that legitimately refreshes multiple stored credentials on a schedule from a single internal host
  • Load/performance testing against a staging Flowise instance
  • A vulnerability scanner fuzzing the credentialId path parameter during an authorized assessment
  • API gateway retry storms replaying the same set of credential IDs after a transient upstream error
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))    // keep only external enumerators; internal bulk-refresh jobs suppressed
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct credentialId path values and their status codes for the offending cIP — a 200/404 mix confirms live enumeration finding valid IDs. Determine whether the source is internal automation or external. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy; upgrade Flowise to 3.1.3; force-rotate every credential whose ID returned HTTP 200 to the attacker. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'burst successful token refresh' on the same cIP to see which tokens were actually exfiltrated, and check connected-service audit logs for use of those tokens.
// Flowise CVE-2026-70478 — credentialId enumeration against the refresh route
W3CIISLog

| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| summarize DistinctCredIds = dcount(csUriStem), TotalRequests = count(), StatusCodes = make_set(scStatus), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 2m)
| where DistinctCredIds >= 5            // 5+ distinct credentialId values in 2 min = enumeration, not a single UI refresh
| order by DistinctCredIds desc
WEB

Flowise burst of successful OAuth2 token refreshes (token harvesting) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects one source obtaining multiple HTTP 200 responses from /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId across distinct credential IDs in a short window — the collection step where an attacker, having enumerated valid IDs, rapidly harvests fresh access tokens for the victims' connected services. Rationale: Targets the advisory's stated impact ('enables token theft for any connected service') by pivoting specifically on HTTP 200 responses (which carry the access_token in tokenInfo) across many credential IDs from one source — distinct from enumeration (which includes 404s) and from a benign single UI refresh. Also flags the DoS-via-quota-exhaustion vector the advisory notes. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/52557
ATT&CKT1528 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled internal automation that legitimately refreshes many Flowise-stored credentials in a batch (internal IP)
  • A power-user admin refreshing several connected-service credentials back-to-back from the console
  • Post-migration or restore job that re-primes all stored OAuth credentials at once
  • Monitoring tooling that periodically validates credential health by refreshing tokens
  • Blue-team validation replaying the exploit in a controlled test window
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))    // suppress internal batch-refresh automation; retain external harvesters
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the credentialIds that returned 200 to this cIP and map each to its connected service and owning workspace/user. Treat every one as a compromised token. 2) Contain: upgrade to Flowise 3.1.3; revoke/rotate the client_secret and refresh_token for every affected credential in the OAuth provider; block the source IP; if quota exhaustion is observed, coordinate token re-issuance with the provider. 3) Hunt: in each connected service's audit log (AAD SigninLogs, Google Workspace, GitHub audit, Slack), search for the leaked tokens being used from the attacker IP or new user-agents, and review whether the same actor also exploited CVE-2026-69250 (SSRF) on the host.
// Flowise CVE-2026-70478 — burst of successful (HTTP 200) token refreshes = token harvesting
W3CIISLog

| where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| where scStatus == 200

| where SuccessfulRefreshes >= 5        // 5+ successful token issuances in 5 min from one source = harvesting
| order by SuccessfulRefreshes desc

Flowise node.js process spawns shell/Python interpreter (CVE-2026-70477 CSV Agent RCE payoff) AIExploitation High
Hunts the execution payoff of the Flowise CSV Agent prompt-injection RCE: the Flowise Node.js server process spawning an OS shell or interpreter child. Because the CSV Agent runs generated Python inside an in-process pyodide WASM runtime, a real sh/bash/python child under a flowise-node parent is anomalous and indicates the blocklist validator was bypassed and code reached OS interfaces. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core mechanism: CSV Agent executes LLM-generated Python in an unsandboxed pyodide (in-process WASM) runtime, so legitimate operation never forks an OS shell/python child from the flowise node parent — any such child is the RCE payoff. Parent=node + commandline contains 'flowise' is the discriminator from generic Node apps. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5xvg-pmgg-3mxr
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Flowise custom-tool / Function node that intentionally shells out (e.g. a user-built ExecutePython or shell tool)
  • Container entrypoint or npm lifecycle scripts spawning sh during flowise startup/build
  • Admin running flowise CLI maintenance that forks bash for migrations
  • Health-check or supervisor scripts (pm2, forever) wrapping the node process
  • Custom document-loader nodes invoking curl/wget for legitimate data fetch
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pm2","npm run","node_modules/.bin","typeorm migration") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; confirm the node parent is the Flowise server (folder path under node_modules/flowise) and not a custom user tool. Decode any obfuscated Python (chr()/concatenation) in nearby app logs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Flowise service, rotate any secrets reachable by the service account (DATABASE creds, OPENAI_API_KEY, FLOWISE_SECRETKEY). 3) Hunt: search the reverse-proxy logs for the preceding POST to /api/v1/prediction/* from the same source IP, and check for outbound connections or new files written by the spawned child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flowise"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "flowise"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High-volume POST to Flowise /api/v1/prediction endpoint (CSV Agent injection probing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts repeated unauthenticated POSTs to the Flowise chatflow prediction endpoint from a single source. The advisory notes prompt-injection 'may take multiple attempts or require a different injection technique depending on the model', so bypass attempts against the CSV Agent surface as a burst of prediction requests from one client — abnormal for a typically single-tenant Flowise deployment. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route from the advisory (CSV Agent invoked via the chatflow prediction endpoint /api/v1/prediction/<id>) combined with a per-source burst threshold matching the 'multiple attempts' language for prompt-injection bypass. Kept hunting-tier because HTTP metadata alone cannot see the CSV body; pair with UC1 for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5xvg-pmgg-3mxr
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate high-frequency chatbot usage or load-testing against a shared Flowise instance
  • An embedded website widget fanning many end-user chats through one egress NAT IP
  • Automated eval/regression harness hitting the prediction API in a loop
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring polling a chatflow
  • Retry storms from a client on transient 5xx responses
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0")   // replace with known app-egress / monitoring IPs after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the top source IPs and user-agents; confirm whether the source is an expected app/NAT egress or an unknown external client, and whether requests hit the CSV Agent chatflow id. 2) Contain: if unauthenticated exposure is confirmed, put Flowise behind auth/allow-list or take the prediction endpoint off the public internet; block the source IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/timeframe against UC1 (node spawning a shell) and check app logs for repeated 'Generated code was rejected for security reasons' rejections.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/prediction/"
| summarize request_count = count(), urls = make_set(RequestURL, 10), agents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where request_count >= 20   // single-user Flowise rarely exceeds ~20 predictions/10min; tune per deployment
| sort by request_count desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count as request_count values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND Web.url="*/api/v1/prediction/*" by _time span=10m Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where request_count >= 20
| sort - request_count
| tstats summariesonly=false count as request_count values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND Web.url="*/api/v1/prediction/*" by _time span=10m Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where request_count >= 20
| sort - request_count
Flowise Python code validator rejection spike (blocklist bypass probing) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Flowise application log signature emitted when the CSV Agent's pythonCodeValidator rejects generated code: 'Generated code was rejected for security reasons'. A cluster of these from one instance indicates an actor iterating obfuscation variants (chr(), __subclasses__, __mro__, df.query(), @exec decorator) to defeat the static regex blocklist described in the advisory. Rationale: Uses the verbatim error string thrown by the vulnerable code path in CSVAgent.ts when validatePythonCodeForDataFrame fails. Repeated rejections are the clearest server-side fingerprint of an actor iterating the eight documented blocklist-bypass variants before one succeeds. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5xvg-pmgg-3mxr
ATT&CKT1190 T1027
Data sourcesApplication_State.All_Application_State
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign users whose natural-language questions cause the LLM to emit non-pandas code that the validator legitimately rejects
  • A poorly-tuned or small local model (e.g. ChatOllama) frequently producing invalid code
  • Developers testing/red-teaming their own chatflow with security controls enabled
  • Prompt-template changes causing a transient uptick in rejected generations
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the surrounding app-log lines to recover the rejected pythonCode and the originating chatflow/session; look for obfuscation tokens (chr(, __subclasses__, __mro__, df.query, __build_class__). 2) Contain: disable the affected CSV Agent chatflow or upgrade flowise / flowise-components beyond 3.1.2 (CVE-2026-70477 fixed); restrict the prediction endpoint to authenticated users. 3) Hunt: correlate the same window against UC1 (node spawning a shell = a variant that PASSED the validator) and UC2 (request burst from the same source IP).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ProcessName has "flowise" or SyslogMessage has "flowise"
| where SyslogMessage has "Generated code was rejected for security reasons"
| summarize rejections = count(), sample = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where rejections >= 3   // repeated validator rejections = active bypass probing; a single miss is benign LLM output
| sort by rejections desc
source:linux.syslog "Generated code was rejected for security reasons"
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=*flowise* OR source=*flowise* "Generated code was rejected for security reasons"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count as rejections, values(host) as hosts by _time
| where rejections >= 3
| sort - _time
Post-RCE secret/config access or egress by Flowise node-parented child AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts post-exploitation of CVE-2026-70477: a child process spawned by the Flowise Node.js server reading Flowise secrets/config (~/.flowise, database.sqlite, .env, FLOWISE_/DATABASE_/API_KEY env) or exfiltrating via curl/wget/nc. Full unsandboxed code execution grants the service account access to stored credentials, chat history, and API keys. Rationale: Chains the RCE (UC1) to concrete collection/exfil by keying on Flowise's real on-disk secret stores (~/.flowise, database.sqlite, .env) and its env-var naming (FLOWISE_/DATABASE_/API_KEY), scoped to children of the flowise node parent so it fires only on post-exploitation, not routine app I/O. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5xvg-pmgg-3mxr
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup jobs copying database.sqlite or the ~/.flowise directory
  • Admin exporting chatflows or reading .env during troubleshooting
  • A custom Flowise tool node that legitimately fetches remote data via curl/wget
  • Config-management (Ansible/Chef) reading env files under the service account
  • Container log/secret sidecars accessing /proc/self/environ
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","ansible","pg_dump") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and the destination (file read vs. network egress); confirm the parent is the Flowise server process and the accessed path holds real secrets. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop Flowise, and immediately rotate every credential the service account could read — DATABASE creds, FLOWISE_SECRETKEY, and all provider API keys (OpenAI/Anthropic/etc.). 3) Hunt: pivot on the egress destination IP/domain across the fleet, review outbound proxy logs for uploads, and confirm patching to flowise/flowise-components > 3.1.2.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flowise"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","curl","wget","nc","ncat","scp","sh","bash","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".flowise","database.sqlite",".env","FLOWISE_","DATABASE_","API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","/proc/self/environ","secretKey")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

Chrome launched with DevTools/remote-debugging port by shell launcher (XCSSET v40 browser hijack) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Chrome hijacker, which wraps the legitimate Google Chrome binary in a malicious launcher script and starts it with Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) enabled on a local port to fetch attacker JavaScript, intercept cookies/credentials, and manipulate MetaMask transactions. Detection keys on Chrome being started with --remote-debugging-port/--remote-debugging-pipe by a shell/osascript parent rather than the user's Finder/launchd session. Rationale: Uses the article's specific Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) hijack behaviour plus Unit 42's detail that the module wraps the Chrome binary in a malicious launcher; the shell/osascript-or-/tmp parent + non-headless remote-debugging flag is the fidelity anchor that separates it from developer automation. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1185 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium end-to-end tests that spawn Chrome with a debugging port (usually --headless, filtered)
  • QA/automation harness launched from a shell script for UI testing
  • Browser extension developer manually starting Chrome with --remote-debugging-port for local debugging
  • Electron/CEF app tooling invoking Chromium with a debugging port from a wrapper shell
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver") and ProcessCommandLine !has "--headless"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the launcher script path (/tmp or /var/folders) — a legit debug session comes from a known dev tool, XCSSET's launcher is an ad hoc-signed script in a temp path. Check the same host's DeviceNetworkEvents for the XCSSET C2 domains/IPs. 2) Contain: kill the Chrome + launcher process, isolate the host, and force a Chrome profile/cookie + password reset (session cookies and MetaMask data are assumed stolen). 3) Hunt: search for /tmp/r, /tmp/p.app, ~/.tr and tccutil reset / CloudTelemetryService activity on the host and across other developer endpoints that pulled the same Xcode project/repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Google Chrome" or FolderPath has "Google Chrome.app"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--headless"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/var/folders/"
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "Google Chrome"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has "--headless"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("bash","zsh","sh","osascript") or ParentProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| where not(ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS security tooling sabotage: tccutil reset + CloudTelemetryService kill + XProtect/softwareupdate tamper (XCSSET v40) AIInstallation High
Hunts XCSSET v40's aggressive defense-evasion stage that resets the TCC database (tccutil reset AppleEvents), terminates Apple's CloudTelemetryService, disables Gatekeeper (spctl), and blocks XProtect/MRT updates via the SoftwareUpdate channel. These commands rarely co-occur in normal user activity and are a strong, article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchors on Unit 42's verbatim evasion actions — tccutil reset AppleEvents, killing CloudTelemetryService, and blocking XProtect/MRT via the SoftwareUpdate channel — which are individually rare and collectively near-unique to this malware's teardown of macOS defenses. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/support running 'tccutil reset' to fix a stuck privacy prompt
  • Developer disabling Gatekeeper with spctl --master-disable to test an unsigned build
  • MDM/management tooling adjusting SoftwareUpdate/XProtect settings during patch policy changes
  • Troubleshooting scripts killing Apple daemons to clear a hung telemetry/update state
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("osascript","bash","sh","zsh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process — legit admin actions come from Terminal/osascript run by a known admin, XCSSET's come from /tmp or /var/folders loaders; check whether tccutil reset, CloudTelemetryService kill, and XProtect tamper cluster within minutes on one host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, re-enable Gatekeeper (spctl --master-enable), and treat the endpoint as fully compromised (defenses were deliberately blinded). 3) Hunt: pivot on /tmp/r, /tmp/p.app, Chrome remote-debugging launches, and the C2 IOCs; check other developers who cloned the same Xcode project/GitHub repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "tccutil" and ProcessCommandLine has "reset")
    or (FileName in~ ("killall","pkill","kill") and ProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService")
    or (FileName =~ "spctl" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--master-disable","--global-disable"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "softwareupdate" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("XProtect","XProtectFramework","MRTConfigData"))
    or ProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "tccutil" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "reset")
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("killall","pkill") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService")
    or (TargetProcessName has "spctl" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--master-disable","--global-disable"))
    or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "softwareupdate" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("XProtect","MRTConfigData"))
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 C2 beacon to Unit 42 IOC domains / IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections and DNS lookups from macOS hosts to the XCSSET v40 command-and-control domains and IPs published by Unit 42. High-confidence IOC match confirmed by multiple second sources reporting the same campaign infrastructure. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the article's pre-extracted C2 domains and IPs, cross-confirmed against the Unit 42 report and secondary write-ups; the impersonation theme (apple*/amzn*/cdn* on .ru/.in TLDs) matches the campaign's fake-CDN infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating an XCSSET sample from a corporate network
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving IOC domains for validation
  • A sinkholed domain now resolving to a benign parking IP (validate the resolved IP)
  • Typosquat collision where a benign internal tool happens to query a lookalike CDN domain (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the endpoint (DeviceNetworkEvents InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect osascript, a /tmp loader, or the wrapped Chrome; confirm the host isn't a sandbox/research box. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at proxy+firewall, isolate the host, and revoke any credentials/session cookies used from it. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the full IOC set, and pull the XCSSET on-host artifacts (/tmp/r, /tmp/p.app, ~/.tr, tccutil/CloudTelemetryService tamper) to scope the intrusion and find the source Xcode project.
let c2domains = dynamic(["amzndev.in","amzndev.ru","googlenets.ru","netcdndev.in","whitead.in","whiteads.ru","accapple.ru","adschecks.ru","adsmobi.ru","adsmorein.in","adsmoreme.in","amdcdn.ru","amznprod.in","applecdn.ru","appledisk.ru","appledns.ru","applehosts.ru","appletime.in","bulksec.ru","cdnamz.in"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2domains = dynamic(["amzndev.in","amzndev.ru","googlenets.ru","netcdndev.in","whitead.in","whiteads.ru","accapple.ru","adschecks.ru","adsmobi.ru","adsmorein.in","adsmoreme.in","amdcdn.ru","amznprod.in","applecdn.ru","appledisk.ru","appledns.ru","applehosts.ru","appletime.in","bulksec.ru","cdnamz.in"]);

XCSSET v40 Telegram trojanizer: /Applications/Telegram.app replacement + ~/.tr config drop AIInstallation High
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Telegram trojanizer, which deletes the legitimate Telegram Desktop app, drops a C2-controlled ad hoc-signed replacement into /Applications/Telegram.app, and writes its state to ~/.tr and ~/.tr_map. Detection keys on non-Telegram, shell/downloader processes modifying the Telegram bundle plus the malware's hidden config files. Rationale: Uses Unit 42's exact artifacts — the /Applications/Telegram.app replacement plus the ~/.tr and ~/.tr_map config files — and requires a shell/downloader (not Telegram's own updater) as the acting process, which is what distinguishes the trojanization from a legitimate Telegram update. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1554 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Telegram Desktop self-update (filtered — acting process is Telegram/softwareupdated, not a shell)
  • User reinstalling Telegram by unzipping a downloaded DMG/zip via Finder/ditto
  • Homebrew cask upgrade of telegram writing to /Applications/Telegram.app
  • Backup/sync tool touching the Telegram bundle path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","softwareupdated","installd") and (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/var/folders/" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("osascript","curl","ditto"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the acting process and command line — a shell/curl/osascript from /tmp writing the Telegram bundle is malicious; verify code signature of the resulting /Applications/Telegram.app (XCSSET's is ad hoc-signed, not Apple/Telegram Developer ID). 2) Contain: kill the process, quarantine the trojanized Telegram.app and ~/.tr*, isolate the host, and warn the user their Telegram session may be intercepted. 3) Hunt: correlate with the Chrome remote-debugging hijack, tccutil/CloudTelemetryService tamper, and C2 IOCs on the same host; check other developer machines for the same Telegram.app replacement pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FolderPath has "/Applications/Telegram.app" and ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified"))
    or FileName in~ (".tr",".tr_map")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript","curl","ditto","unzip","tar") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/var/folders/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","softwareupdated","installd","Install Telegram")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "/Applications/Telegram.app") or TargetFileName in~ (".tr",".tr_map")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript","curl","ditto","unzip","tar") or ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| where ActingProcessName !has "Telegram"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 build-time execution: Xcode-spawned osascript loader / /tmp/r payload AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 initial execution that triggers when a developer builds a compromised Xcode project: an injected script launches an in-memory osascript loader that pulls the orchestrator, and the malware stages a loader at /tmp/r and an AppleScript wrapper at /tmp/p.app. Detection keys on Xcode/xcodebuild spawning osascript, or any process referencing the /tmp/r and /tmp/p.app loader paths. Rationale: Uses Unit 42's verbatim loader paths (/tmp/r primary loader, /tmp/p.app AppleScript wrapper) and the article's core mechanic that an in-memory osascript loader runs when a poisoned Xcode project is built; osascript spawned by Xcode/xcodebuild is abnormal for normal build phases (which use /bin/sh). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Xcode build 'Run Script' phase that intentionally calls osascript (e.g. to display a notification)
  • Developer tooling or Fastlane lanes invoking osascript during a build
  • A benign local script that happens to use a /tmp/r or /tmp/p.app path name (rare)
  • CI runner on macOS executing AppleScript automation as part of packaging
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "osascript" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("fastlane","display notification","display dialog"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the osascript command line and parent Xcode project path; dump /tmp/r and /tmp/p.app for analysis and check the project's benign files/Git hooks for the injected downloader script. 2) Contain: isolate the developer host, kill the loader chain, and freeze the source repository/branch to stop propagation to other developers. 3) Hunt: identify every developer who cloned or built the same project/repo, and sweep those hosts for the Chrome hijack, Telegram replacement, security-tamper commands, and C2 IOCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/r","/tmp/p.app")
    or FolderPath in~ ("/tmp/r")
    or (FileName =~ "osascript" and (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Xcode.app"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/r","/tmp/p.app")
    or (TargetProcessName has "osascript" and (ParentProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ParentProcessName has "Xcode.app"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: XCSSET v40 Xcode Build-Time osascript Loader / tmp Payload
id: c6b1f2a8-5d90-4a6e-8b71-2a9f0e3c47d2
description: Detects XCSSET v40 build-triggered execution - osascript spawned by Xcode/xcodebuild or processes referencing the /tmp/r loader and /tmp/p.app AppleScript wrapper.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-xcsset-variant-targets-macos-devs-via-compromised-xcode-projects/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1059.002
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: macos
detection:
  sel_tmp:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/tmp/r'
      - '/tmp/p.app'
  sel_osascript:
    Image|endswith: '/osascript'
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'xcodebuild'
      - 'Xcode.app'
  condition: sel_tmp or sel_osascript
level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (CommandLine=/\/tmp\/r(\s|$)/i OR CommandLine=/\/tmp\/p\.app/i OR (ImageFileName=/osascript$/i AND ParentImageFileName=/(xcodebuild|Xcode\.app)/i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/tmp/r*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/p.app*" OR (Processes.process_name="osascript" AND (Processes.parent_process_name="xcodebuild" OR Processes.parent_process="*Xcode.app*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/tmp/r*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/p.app*" OR (Processes.process_name="osascript" AND (Processes.parent_process_name="xcodebuild" OR Processes.parent_process="*Xcode.app*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |

    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:

            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'

        Image|endswith:

            - '\Exodus.exe'

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d") or SHA1 in~ ("6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d") or MD5 in~ ("6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d") or SHA1 in~ ("6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d") or MD5 in~ ("6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6e480d648fa1b70612f5d198a66875e28847547d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — 77 Open VSX extensions found harvesting developer info

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Code editor / node extension-host resolving mangorbit[.]com (evil-twin attribution) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Open VSX evil-twin extension exfiltration to mangorbit[.]com C2 infrastructure AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to mangorbit.com or its subdomains (pulse, pulse2, api, cb.*), the single exfiltration domain shared by all 77 counterfeit Open VSX developer-tool extensions. Because the domain was registered 11 days before the campaign and is used exclusively by these malicious packages, any contact is high-fidelity evidence of an installed evil-twin extension. Rationale: Anchors on mangorbit.com (and pulse/pulse2/api/cb subdomains) — the single exfil domain Manifold links all 77 packages through, registered 2026-07-15, 11 days pre-campaign. `has "mangorbit"` token-matches every subdomain including the randomized cb.* ones. Domain is single-source (Manifold/BleepingComputer) but its exclusivity and fresh registration make any contact high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/77-open-vsx-extensions-found-harvesting-developer-info/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/glassworm-supply-chain-attack-abuses-72.html • https://socket.dev/blog/glassworm-sleeper-extensions-activated-on-open-vsx
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1176.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • Malware-analysis sandbox or detonation VM resolving the IOC during sample triage
  • Threat-intel enrichment host (urlscan/VirusTotal-style scanner) auto-resolving the domain from an IOC feed
  • SOAR playbook performing automated IOC enrichment/lookup of mangorbit.com
  • Post-takedown sinkhole/NXDOMAIN attempts still generating DNS log entries after the domain was pulled 2026-08-03
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving/connecting host and the InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm it is a code editor (Code.exe/Cursor.exe/node.exe) and not a sandbox/TI-enrichment host. Pull the developer's installed Open VSX extension list and match IDs against Manifold's report. 2) Contain: block mangorbit.com at DNS/proxy/firewall org-wide; on the affected host uninstall the counterfeit extension and remove it from workspace .vscode/extensions.json recommendation configs. 3) Hunt: sweep all dev endpoints for the same domain, review .git remote hosts / CI tokens (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Buildkite, CircleCI, Codespaces, Gitpod) that were readable in exposed workspaces, and rotate any CI identifiers that could have been profiled.

(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has "mangorbit" or RequestURL has "mangorbit" | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), DnsQueryTypeName="", Source="Proxy", EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct)

Code editor / node extension-host resolving mangorbit[.]com (evil-twin attribution) AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates hosts that both run a VS Code-family editor (Code/Cursor/Windsurf/VSCodium/node extension host) and resolve mangorbit.com, attributing the exfiltration to the malicious extension running inside the editor rather than a coincidental IOC hit. Scopes the alert to developer workstations and confirms the extension-host process as the initiator, and covers the DNS-based fallback channel the malware uses when hardcoded infrastructure is unreachable. Rationale: Ties the mangorbit.com contact to the editor extension-host process (Code/Cursor/Windsurf/VSCodium/node) — the article states the payload runs inside the extension host and sends data ~4-5s after activation, and falls back to a DNS TXT lookup for a replacement URL when hardcoded infra is down. Process attribution both raises fidelity over the pure-network hit and scopes the hunt to developer workstations. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/77-open-vsx-extensions-found-harvesting-developer-info/ • https://socket.dev/blog/glassworm-loader-hits-open-vsx-via-suspected-developer-account-compromise
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568.002 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually resolving/testing the mangorbit.com IOC from a terminal inside VS Code
  • Security team running Manifold's own detection/verification script from a dev workstation
  • node.exe on a build agent resolving the domain during an unrelated dependency fetch that a proxy rewrote
  • Post-takedown NXDOMAIN retries logged from the extension host before the extension is removed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a code-editor/extension host and enumerate that user's Open VSX extensions (version 0.0.1 low-version counterfeits, unrelated publisher namespaces impersonating AMD/Azure/Salesforce/Hyperledger/LEGO Education/IOTA). 2) Contain: uninstall the offending extension, purge it from the host and any shared workspace .vscode config, and DNS-block mangorbit.com. 3) Hunt: check for randomized subdomains under cb.mangorbit.com and DNS TXT queries (fallback-channel resolution) from the same host, and review which Git/CI metadata (remote hosts, org, configured-email domain, branch, HEAD hash, CI/cloud-dev identifiers) the extension could have profiled.

128 Seconds to disruption: Microsoft Defender stops ransomware at QNET

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-08-04 9 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Defender automatically isolated a compromised QNET endpoint in 128 seconds, stopping a multi-stage attack before the payload could persist or spread. The post 128 Seconds to disruption: Microsoft Defender stops ransomware at QNET appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1057 T1059 T1071.001 T1105 T1112 T1190 T1204 T1204.002 T1218.005 T1486
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] mshta.exe retrieving remote second-stage payload via URL or script protocol
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RunMRU Run-dialog key populated with mshta / URL / LOLBin command · [LLM] Multi-stage chain: mshta execution followed by RunMRU write on same host · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] mshta.exe making outbound connection to a public IP · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
mshta.exe retrieving remote second-stage payload via URL or script protocol AIDelivery High
Hunts the QNET entry step: a signed Windows binary (mshta.exe) invoked with an http(s) URL or inline vbscript:/javascript: protocol to proxy-execute an attacker-hosted second stage. Article-specific because the intrusion began with mshta.exe pulling a remote payload rather than a local .hta. Rationale: Uses the article's named LOLBin (mshta.exe) plus the reported behaviour of contacting an attacker-controlled URL to retrieve a second stage; mshta with a URL/script-protocol arg is very rare in benign use. Cross-checked MITRE T1218.005 and existing SigmaHQ proc_creation_win_mshta_http. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/ • https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_mshta_http.yml • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/techniques/mshta/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal LOB apps launched via HTA hosted on an intranet URL
  • Admin/help-desk scripts that call `mshta vbscript:...` for legacy dialog prompts
  • Software deployment tooling that stages .hta from a UNC share
  • Security-team red-team or purple-team exercises reusing the mshta technique
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (".corp.",".local","intranet"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and resolve the remote URL/host; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the mshta-initiated connection and whether the payload was retrieved (HTTP 200 / bytes). 2) Contain: if the domain is unknown/newly-seen, isolate the host (or confirm Defender attack-disruption already did) and block the URL/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for RunMRU writes and any child processes spawned by mshta within 5 minutes; sweep the org for other hosts contacting the same remote host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","vbscript:","javascript:","\\\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","vbscript:","javascript:","\\\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mshta.exe making outbound connection to a public IP AICommand & Control Medium
Detects mshta.exe — a binary that almost never legitimately reaches the internet — opening an outbound connection to a public address, matching the article's step where mshta.exe contacted attacker-controlled infrastructure over web protocols to pull the second stage. Rationale: Article states mshta.exe initiated outbound HTTP/HTTPS to attacker-controlled infra (T1071.001); a signed system utility egressing to a public IP is a high-signal LOLBin pair. Sentinel left empty because the listed ASIM/Sentinel tables carry no reliable initiating-process attribution for network sessions (ImNetworkSession lacks process fields) — the process-attributed egress lives only in MDE/Sysmon. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/efbcf8ee-bc75-47f1-8985-a5c638c4faf0/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1218.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intranet HTA apps whose backend resolves to a public/cloud-hosted IP
  • Endpoint management agents that shell out to mshta against a SaaS URL
  • Proxy/PAC misconfiguration routing internal HTA fetches over a public egress
  • Red-team infrastructure testing during authorised exercises
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any (".corp.",".internal","intranet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich RemoteIP/RemoteUrl against threat intel and org first-seen; correlate with the mshta ProcessCommandLine that opened the socket. 2) Contain: block the destination at the egress proxy/firewall and isolate the host if the destination is unknown or the payload transferred. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for mshta.exe connecting to the same IP/ASN, and check for follow-on child processes and RunMRU persistence writes on the affected host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RunMRU Run-dialog key populated with mshta / URL / LOLBin command AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the article's observed RunMRU persistence/execution artifact: the Explorer\RunMRU key holding a command line referencing mshta, a remote URL, or another LOLBin — the fingerprint of a ClickFix-style Run-dialog abuse or scripted persistence rather than a benign typed command. Rationale: RunMRU is named twice in the article as the observed user-level persistence artifact; scoping to value data that contains mshta/URL/LOLBin tokens separates malicious Run-dialog abuse from ordinary typed paths. Datadog query cannot filter on value data (Sysmon Details not in the tagged schema) so it matches all RunMRU writes and is flagged hunting-grade there. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112/ • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/techniques/mshta/
ATT&CKT1112 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A power user legitimately typing a UNC path or `cmd` into the Run dialog
  • Admins launching PowerShell one-liners via Win+R during troubleshooting
  • Software that pre-seeds RunMRU with an installer/updater command
  • Remote-support tooling driving the Run box to launch diagnostics
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any ("\\\\fileserver\\","\\\\dfs\\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and RegistryValueData !has_any ("http","mshta"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full RegistryValueData and the writing process; determine whether the referenced binary/URL executed (correlate DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceNetworkEvents within ~5 min on the same host). 2) Contain: if the command references an unknown URL or LOLBin fetch, isolate the host and capture the RunMRU value for IR. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same RunMRU command string across the fleet (worm/lure reuse) and check for mshta execution and outbound connections on matching hosts.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","http://","https://","powershell","cmd /c","cmd.exe","certutil","regsvr32","bitsadmin","wscript","cscript","\\\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has "RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","http://","https://","powershell","cmd /c","cmd.exe","certutil","regsvr32","bitsadmin","wscript","cscript","\\\\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: RunMRU Run-Dialog Key Populated With Mshta or LOLBin Command

Multi-stage chain: mshta execution followed by RunMRU write on same host AIInstallation High
High-fidelity correlation of the exact QNET sequence — mshta.exe executing (as parent or child) and a RunMRU registry write on the same device within a 5-minute window. Ties the LOLBin second-stage execution to the user-level persistence artifact, which neither single-event rule captures alone. Rationale: Encodes the article's precise timeline (mshta execution then RunMRU interaction seconds apart); the temporal same-host join makes it far higher fidelity than either single event and is the article's distinguishing signature. Sigma/Datadog omitted because this is a cross-table time-window correlation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/129-seconds-disruption-microsoft-defender-stops-ransomware-qnet/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user launching an HTA via the Run dialog then typing another command (both benign) within 5 min
  • Admin troubleshooting session that runs mshta and later uses Win+R
  • Automated software packaging that both invokes mshta and seeds RunMRU
  • Purple-team exercise replaying the mshta+RunMRU chain
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","http","powershell","cmd","certutil","regsvr32")
Response runbook
1) Triage: reconstruct the process tree around the mshta event and read the correlated RunMRU value; confirm whether mshta fetched a remote payload (network events same host/window). 2) Contain: isolate the device (verify Defender attack-disruption did not already isolate) and preserve the RunMRU value + any dropped .hta/second-stage files. 3) Hunt: extract the remote URL/host and RunMRU command, then sweep the org for the same strings and for other hosts showing the mshta→RunMRU pairing.
let Window = 5m;
let RunMRU = DeviceRegistryEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
    | project RegTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "mshta.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner RunMRU on DeviceId
| where RegTime between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + Window)
| project Timestamp, RegTime, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 5m;
let RunMRU = ImRegistryEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RegistryKey has "RunMRU"
    | project RegTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryValueData;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "mshta.exe" or TargetProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| join kind=inner RunMRU on DvcHostname
| where RegTime between (TimeGenerated .. TimeGenerated + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, RegTime, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\mshta\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegObjectName=/RunMRU/i | rename(RegStringValue, as=RunMRUValue)}, field=aid, include=[RunMRUValue, RegObjectName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, RunMRUValue], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as procTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=mshta.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as regTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Explorer\\RunMRU*" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`] | eval delta=abs(regTime-procTime) | where delta<=300 | table dest user procTime regTime delta registry_value_data | sort - procTime
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as procTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=mshta.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as regTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Explorer\\RunMRU*" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`] | eval delta=abs(regTime-procTime) | where delta<=300 | table dest user procTime regTime delta registry_value_data | sort - procTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
