Powercat fake Xeno loader chain (xeno.exe → AppData javaw.exe → decompiler.exe) AIDelivery High
Hunts the Bitdefender/ThreatLocker-tracked Powercat infection chain delivered via fake Xeno Roblox executor: a xeno.exe first stage that extracts a bundled JRE and runs javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin, then launches an Allatori-obfuscated JAR masquerading as decompiler.exe. Rationale: Uses the article's named stages (xeno.exe, decompiler.exe) plus the Bitdefender/BleepingComputer-confirmed bundled-JRE path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe; a decompiler.exe that is actually a JAR and a Java runtime under a user AppData path are both strongly anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/ • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer with a portable/embedded JRE under AppData running javaw.exe for a legitimate tool
  • A build/CI tool named decompiler.exe used by reverse-engineering staff
  • Minecraft/modding launchers that bundle their own JRE in AppData
  • Portable Java IDE plugins launched from a user profile
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("minecraftlauncher.exe","javaw.exe") and FolderPath has @"\.minecraft\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the javaw.exe path is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin and check for a sibling XenoIcon.jpg (key file) and decompiler.exe JAR; hash the parent xeno.exe. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the java processes, and remove the AppData\Java staging and the GameDVR payload directory. 3) Hunt: pivot to solthere.net C2 (UC6) and the 'Display Calibration' Run-key persistence (UC7), then scope credential/wallet-theft on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "javaw.exe" and FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "xeno.exe"
     or FileName =~ "decompiler.exe"
     or (FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "decompiler")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "javaw.exe" and ActingProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\")
     or ParentProcessName has "xeno.exe"
     or ActingProcessName has "decompiler.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat stage-2 C2 to solthere.net redeem endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network activity to the Powercat stage-2 command-and-control domain solthere.net (observed path /api/v1/redeem for pulling the next-stage payload with an AES+Base64 key). Any internal host resolving this domain is a strong Powercat indicator. Rationale: solthere.net is the article's named Powercat C2 domain, independently confirmed by Bitdefender (redeem endpoint /api/v1/redeem) and BleepingComputer; a bare domain match on a rarely-benign infrastructure name is high-fidelity and alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or analyst VM detonating the sample and resolving the C2
  • Security scanner/crawler pre-fetching IOC domains for enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging a blocked lookup (still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and initiating process — javaw.exe from an AppData JRE (UC5) confirms Powercat. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block solthere.net at protective DNS, isolate the host, and terminate the java stealer processes. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Display Calibration' Run key (UC7), the GameDVR payload directory, and browser/wallet/Discord credential access indicative of stage-3 theft.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "solthere.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "solthere.net"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat stage-3 persistence via HKCU Run 'Display Calibration' → GameDVR payload AIInstallation High
Hunts the Powercat stage-3 persistence mechanism: an HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value named 'Display Calibration' (or any Run value pointing into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR) that auto-runs the fake-named DLL payload at logon. Rationale: Bitdefender confirmed the exact persistence artifact: HKCU\...\Run value 'Display Calibration' pointing at a fake DLL in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR. The masquerading value name plus the GameDVR path make this a single-event, near-zero-FP persistence detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate display-calibration utility that genuinely registers a Run entry (rare; verify the target path is not GameDVR)
  • GameDVR/Xbox Game Bar legitimately writing to its own directory (but not via a Run key with this value name)
  • Endpoint-management tooling seeding benign Run keys during imaging
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR\" or RegistryValueName =~ "Display Calibration"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — a Run value named 'Display Calibration' launching a DLL from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR (typically via rundll32/regsvr32) is confirmed Powercat. 2) Contain: delete the Run value, isolate the host, and remove the GameDVR payload; reset credentials for browser/Discord/crypto-wallet apps that may have been harvested. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC5 (loader chain) and UC6 (solthere.net C2) and sweep other gaming endpoints for the same Run value.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Display Calibration"
     or RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Display Calibration"
     or RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"

`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent

Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-04 16 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Nearly half of C2 malware bypasses DNS by connecting directly to IP addresses. Zero trust IP enforcement secures networks against these threats. The post Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phorpiex dropper D2IP payload retrieval from 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SectopRAT in-browser proxy /churl traffic mirroring to attacker IPs · [LLM] Hardcoded WebSocket backdoor to 154.92.19.71:39989 (no DNS) · [LLM] ZT-IP hunt: direct-to-IP egress with no preceding DNS resolution · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Custom \GET obfuscated exfiltration to 18.228.188.56 / SHA256-tracked sample · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phorpiex dropper D2IP payload retrieval from 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts direct-to-IP HTTP GETs to the Phorpiex/Trik staging host 178.16.54.109, which serves loaders (st.exe, 32.exe/64.exe, twizt.exe, xmrig.exe) and staged config paths (/1../6, /sex/k/n.txt, /new.php). Article-specific because the IP is a confirmed long-running Phorpiex delivery node contacted with no preceding DNS query. Rationale: IP 178.16.54.109 is a confirmed Phorpiex C2/loader host (corroborated by Bitsight and executemalware IOC repo serving 32.exe/64.exe/twizt.exe/xmrig.exe), contacted D2IP with no DNS — a high-fidelity, low-FP anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/ransomware-twizt-inside-phorpiex-botnet • https://github.com/executemalware/Malware-IOCs/blob/main/2024-03-28%20Phorpiex%20IOCs • https://otx.alienvault.com/pulse/606aea55d76b8a0aeccfa377
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox VM detonating samples against the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IP
  • Honeypot or deception host beaconing to the IP by design
  • Shared-hosting reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/timeframe)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\SandBox\", @"\Analysis\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and its SHA256; pull any file written from the host (st.exe/windrv.exe/sysmgnrsv.exe) via DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block 178.16.54.109 at egress, and quarantine the dropped loader. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256 org-wide, XMRig persistence, and Run-key/service autoruns pointing at %userprofile% driver-look-alike names.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "178.16.54.109"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "178.16.54.109"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SectopRAT in-browser proxy /churl traffic mirroring to attacker IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts SectopRAT (ArechClient2) in-browser proxy beacons to 87.120.107.33 and 194.76.227.94, and the /churl endpoint that relays every visited URL (including authenticated session pages) to the operator. Article-specific because two distinct actors deployed the same family against education using these exact IPs and the /churl proxy path. Rationale: Two named SectopRAT proxy IPs plus the malware-specific /churl relay path give an IP-and-path double anchor; SectopRAT's browser-proxy/BrowserLogging capability is corroborated by Darktrace/G DATA write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/not-your-average-rodent-darktraces-mitigation-of-the-sectop-remote-access-trojan-rat • https://www.gdatasoftware.com/blog/2021/02/36633-new-version-adds-encrypted-communication
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1185 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal API that happens to expose a /churl path (validate against the named IPs)
  • Corporate forward-proxy appliance whose logs mirror URLs (matches /churl only if such a path exists internally)
  • Sandbox detonation of SectopRAT samples by the SOC
  • IP reassignment on shared hosting after the campaign window
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process holding the socket (SectopRAT often injects into or masquerades as a browser/.NET host) and capture its SHA256; review /churl payloads for exfiltrated session URLs. 2) Contain: isolate host, block both IPs, force-reset credentials for any authenticated sessions seen relayed. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents for the injecting .NET binary, secondary desktop creation, and other hosts beaconing to either IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") or RemoteUrl has "/churl"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") or RequestURL has "/churl"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Custom \GET obfuscated exfiltration to 18.228.188.56 / SHA256-tracked sample AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the persistent \GET (backslash-GET) exfiltration campaign: a malformed HTTP method followed by a 250–666 char structured-encoded blob, beaconing to Brazil-cloud IP 18.228.188.56 with rotating ports. Anchored on the named IP and the disassembled sample hash so it survives the actor's IP/port rotation OpSec. Rationale: Dual anchor: the named C2 IP 18.228.188.56 plus the disassembled sample SHA256 cc43cd… — the hash survives the campaign's documented IP/port rotation, and the \GET method string catches proxy-visible variants. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workload hosted in the same AWS sa-east-1 (Brazil) range if the IP is reassigned post-campaign
  • Proxy that URL-encodes methods and false-matches on a backslash before GET
  • SOC malware detonation of the tracked sample
  • Vulnerability scanner malforming HTTP methods against the host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process matches SHA256 cc43cd… and inspect SentBytes / the encoded blob length (250–666 chars) for exfil volume. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the IP, and preserve the process binary for the encoding-scheme keys noted in the article. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 across all hosts, look for the same 250–666 char \GET pattern to other rotating IPs/ports, and scope impacted sectors (gov/airline/university assets).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "18.228.188.56"
   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP == "18.228.188.56" or RequestMethod contains "\\GET"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestMethod, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, SentBytes, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hardcoded WebSocket backdoor to 154.92.19.71:39989 (no DNS) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the backdoor that opens a WebSocket (wss) directly to the Unicode-hardcoded C2 154.92.19.71 on non-standard port 39989 with zero preceding DNS. Article-specific via the exact IP+port pair extracted from the binary via Ghidra. Rationale: Exact IP+port pair (154.92.19.71:39989) reverse-engineered from the binary as a hardcoded Unicode wss:// string; the non-standard high port plus D2IP makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071 T1571 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app legitimately using port 39989 to an unrelated host (excluded by the exact IP match)
  • SOC sandbox detonation of the backdoor
  • Deception/honeypot beacon to the IP
  • IP reassignment after the campaign window
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process opening the socket and its SHA256/parent; confirm no DNS query preceded the connection. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 154.92.19.71:39989 at egress, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: extract other hardcoded Unicode IP strings from the sample, sweep for the same binary hash and any other high-port D2IP beacons org-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "154.92.19.71" and RemotePort == 39989
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "154.92.19.71" and DestinationPort == 39989
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ZT-IP hunt: direct-to-IP egress with no preceding DNS resolution AICommand & Control Medium
Encodes the article's zero-trust-IP method — surfacing outbound public-IP connections that carry no resolved domain context (raw IP, no preceding DNS), initiated by non-browser processes. This is how Unit 42 surfaced the Phorpiex, \GET and SectopRAT infrastructure; it is a broad hunting sweep for new D2IP C2 beyond the named IOCs. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's ZT-IP thesis (RemoteUrl empty + public IP = no sanctioning DNS response) and prioritises the five named C2 IPs while surfacing new D2IP infrastructure; scoped to non-browser processes and a burst floor to manage the acknowledged high FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NTP/time sync and OS telemetry that legitimately dial IPs directly
  • IP-literal CDN/anycast endpoints (some app updaters, game clients)
  • Monitoring/EDR agents beaconing to hardcoded management IPs
  • P2P/collaboration apps (WebRTC, torrent) using direct-IP mesh
  • Software licensing checks that connect by IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","ntoskrnl.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","w3wp.exe") and RemotePort !in (123, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by the KnownBad flag first, then by rare process+IP pairs; pull the initiating binary's SHA256 and signer. 2) Contain: for any KnownC2 or unsigned/rare binary, isolate the host and block the IP. 3) Hunt: baseline the process→IP pairs over 30 days, promote persistent unexplained D2IP beacons to alerting, and cross-check destinations against threat intel.
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe"]);
let KnownC2 = dynamic(["178.16.54.109","18.228.188.56","87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94","154.92.19.71"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl)                       // no domain context => direct-to-IP (ZT-IP)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (Browsers)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName)
          by RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| extend KnownBad = RemoteIP in (KnownC2)
| where KnownBad or Conns > 20                   // 20 = burst floor to cut one-off IP checks
| order by KnownBad desc, FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or SHA1 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or MD5 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or SHA1 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or MD5 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

How legitimate cloud platforms enable phishers to bypass MFA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-08-04 9 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

We cover a cloud-based AitM attack scenario leveraging service workers and Ultraviolet, and provide detailed phishing hosting statistics across platforms like Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, and IPFS.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] First-seen browser egress to abused cloud-PaaS phishing domains (workers.dev / pages.dev / vercel.app / github.io / netlify.app / dweb.link) · [LLM] Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
First-seen browser egress to abused cloud-PaaS phishing domains (workers.dev / pages.dev / vercel.app / github.io / netlify.app / dweb.link) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a corporate browser making its first-ever connection (org-wide baseline anti-join) to a subdomain of the exact free-tier PaaS platforms this campaign abuses to host its AitM CAPTCHA relay and Ultraviolet reverse-proxy pages. Because the parent domains host millions of legit projects, the fidelity comes from the never-before-seen-in-org pivot, not the suffix alone. Rationale: Uses the exact PaaS suffix set from the article's statistics table (pages.dev 24.9%, vercel.app 13.8%, github.io 13.7%, netlify.app 10.0%, dweb.link 7.8%, plus workers.dev from the case study). Baseline anti-join is the noise reducer since these apex domains are shared with legit content. Cross-checked urlscan.io (Ultraviolet campaign) and RingSafe/Cofense Cloudflare-abuse reports. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/ • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.006 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/DevOps staff legitimately visiting a colleague's Cloudflare Pages or Vercel preview deployment
  • Open-source project documentation hosted on github.io
  • IPFS gateway (dweb.link) used by a legitimate web3/crypto app
  • Marketing landing pages a partner hosts on netlify.app
  • SaaS vendor status pages or serverless webhooks on workers.dev
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("devops-svc","builder")) and Devices == 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RemoteUrl/DstHostname and fetch it in a sandbox — a genuine hit shows a fake CAPTCHA gate or a Microsoft login iframe/BitB pop-up with a spoofed address bar. Check whether the same user received an inbound email whose link redirected here. 2) Contain: block the specific FQDN at proxy/DNS (not the apex), reset the user's Entra credentials and revoke all sessions/refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: search that user's SigninLogs for a successful MFA-satisfied sign-in from a datacenter/hosting IP within 30 min (AitM token replay) and check for new inbox rules or OAuth grants.

    | summarize by RemoteUrl;

Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing AIDelivery Medium
Hunts UrlClickEvents where the resolved redirect chain (UrlChain) or final URL lands on one of the campaign's abused PaaS platforms — mirroring the article's Stage 1→2 flow of compromised-site CAPTCHA relay bouncing the victim to a *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy page. Targets the redirect landing, not the innocuous-looking link in the email body. Rationale: Anchors on the article's multi-stage redirect (email link -> compromised site CAPTCHA -> *.workers.dev), so it inspects the Safe Links UrlChain rather than the benign first-hop domain. ClickedThrough is the high-fidelity user-bypass signal. PaaS suffixes taken directly from the article's platform table. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1583.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit newsletter/marketing tracking link that happens to redirect through a Vercel/Netlify edge function
  • Internal app or CI notification linking to a github.io or pages.dev docs page
  • A vendor's URL-shortener whose final hop is a serverless health page
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platforms hosting lures on PaaS
  • Web3 wallet flows resolving through a dweb.link IPFS gateway
Suppression filter
| where IsClickedThrough == true or Workload == "Email"
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the full UrlChain terminal URL; confirm a Microsoft login iframe/BitB window and check whether the redirect emerged from a compromised legitimate first-hop domain. Confirm ActionType/IsClickedThrough (user actually reached the page). 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete the source message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents ZAP, block the terminal FQDN, force credential reset + session revocation for the clicker. 3) Hunt: enumerate other recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/sender, and pivot each clicker into UC-3 to catch AitM session replay.
let PaaS = dynamic(["workers.dev","pages.dev","vercel.app","github.io","netlify.app","dweb.link"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend Chain = tostring(UrlChain)
| where Chain has_any (PaaS) or Url has_any (PaaS)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, UrlChain=Chain, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Workload, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

let PaaS = dynamic(["workers.dev","pages.dev","vercel.app","github.io","netlify.app","dweb.link"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend Chain = tostring(UrlChain)
| where Chain has_any (PaaS) or Url has_any (PaaS)
| project TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, Url, UrlChain=Chain, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Workload, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an endpoint browser connecting to a campaign PaaS domain (Stage 2/3 Ultraviolet proxy + BitB) with a successful, MFA-satisfied Entra sign-in for the same user within 30 minutes whose source IP does NOT match the victim's device — the hallmark of the attacker replaying the intercepted session token from their own infrastructure. This is the payoff step the article describes: credentials and MFA relayed, then the attacker holds a live session. Rationale: Expresses the article's core AitM outcome: MFA relayed through the *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy, then the attacker uses the token from their own IP. The IP-mismatch clause (sign-in source != victim device public IP) within a 30-min window of the PaaS visit is the discriminator corroborated by Cofense/Securelist noting the token is replayed from a different IP/ASN than where the victim authenticated. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1111 T1550.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User visits a legit PaaS-hosted app then signs in to M365 over corporate VPN/egress with a different public IP than the device reports
  • Roaming/mobile user whose device PublicIP and sign-in IP legitimately differ (cellular vs Wi-Fi)
  • CDN/proxy egress that rewrites the outbound IP for O365 traffic
  • Shared-device/kiosk scenarios where DeviceInfo PublicIP is stale
  • Developer testing their own Cloudflare Worker while authenticated to Azure
Suppression filter
| where SignInIP !in (dynamic([])) and Country != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in IP is a hosting/datacenter ASN (not corporate egress or the user's ISP) and that the PaaS URL detonates to a Microsoft login/BitB page — that combination is a confirmed token theft. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens/sessions for the account (Entra 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-registration of MFA; block the SignInIP and PaaS FQDN. 3) Hunt: review AuditLogs/CloudAppEvents for attacker-created inbox forwarding rules, new OAuth app consents, MFA method additions, and mailbox exfiltration under that account after the sign-in time.
let Window = 30m;
let PhishConns = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
    | where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".pages.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".vercel.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".github.io" or RemoteUrl endswith ".netlify.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
    | project ConnTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, PhishUrl=RemoteUrl, UserUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn;
let DevIP = DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, PublicIP) by DeviceName;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SignInTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn, SignInIP=IPAddress, Application, Country, City
| join kind=inner PhishConns on $left.AccountUpn == $right.UserUpn
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| join kind=leftouter DevIP on DeviceName
| where isempty(PublicIP) or SignInIP != PublicIP
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), AccountUpn, DeviceName, PhishUrl, SignInIP, DevicePublicIP=PublicIP, Application, Country, City
| order by SignInTime desc
let Window = 30m;
let Phish = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstHostname endswith ".workers.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".pages.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".vercel.app" or DstHostname endswith ".github.io" or DstHostname endswith ".netlify.app" or DstHostname endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
    | project ConnTime=TimeGenerated, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, PhishHost=DstHostname;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| project SignInTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP=IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Location
| join kind=inner Phish on $left.UserPrincipalName == $right.SrcUsername
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| where SignInIP != SrcIpAddr
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), UserPrincipalName, PhishHost, SignInIP, VictimIP=SrcIpAddr, AppDisplayName, Location
| order by SignInTime desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Deletes 3 ADK AI Workflows After Malicious GitHub Issue Could Trigger Privileged Agent

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 7 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Google deleted three AI agent workflows from its Agent Development Kit (ADK) Python repository. Pillar Security showed that a public GitHub issue could manipulate a triage agent into triggering a privileged code-fixing agent. The researchers said the public agent could be prompt-injected into posting /adk-issue-fix as adk-bot. They identified the bot as a collaborator, so that comment satisfied
